title: Teaching New Orleans style and Wynton Marsalis's program
summary: Traditional jazz can be codified and taught; kids danced to Bourbon Street Parade at yesterday's show.

venues.name: YMCA Center for the Creative Arts

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: Is it hard to teach someone to play in the style of a New Orleans musician? What I’m trying to get at is, you mentioned that in colleges it’s like jazz starts with Charlie Parker.

And they’ve figured out a way, whether we could debate about it or not, they figured out a way to codify what he did, and teach it. But can you codify what a second line is and what those musicians do?

Yeah I think that you can do that in the same way that you could the other styles that they’re doing in the university. I don’t think it’s the same as, like I said, getting the experience on the bandstand. It’s never the same. I mean you can’t get that out of a book, no matter what you’re studying. But when I was in the Y in New York we had a program, I can’t remember the name of it but Wynton Marsalis had put out a great educational program for kids of traditional jazz. And he explained everything. We went through the exercises, explaining like the two-beat feel for the drummer, that marching feel, and that unique New Orleans feel and everything, and traditional jazz tunes, they learned the melody, the chord structure. So it can be done, it’s just a question of the promotion of that. And that’s just not, I mean who makes the decisions on what should be — if Trane should be studied before Louis Armstrong, or why Trane should be studied more than Louis Armstrong — I don’t know who makes, how that comes about. But it’s cool. We just do what we do. And it’s still validating when we’re performing and we see people moving in their seats or who want to get up and dance or want to start clapping on a second line. It means, it’s like Gerald was saying yesterday in our performance, you know we had these little kids who maybe were ten and whatever, and we started playing that “Bourbon Street Parade” with that parade beat, and they were all dancing and moving and shaking. And the teacher was trying to tell them, “no, be still.” You know? And no, the point is for you to move, that’s the whole point.
I know. Doesn’t that make you crazy?
Yeah. And I mean that’s what I mean, yeah. The music is still, it can still move people, it’s just not being promoted to people.
